Nose
NOZE
n.
From Anglo-Saxon nosu. Webster 1828: the prominent part of the face which is the organ of smell. In Hebrew the same word means both nose and anger, since the flaring nostril was the visible sign of wrath, and that connection governs much of the Old Testament’s language about God.

Biblical Definition

The Hebrew aph means nose, nostril, and anger, and the double sense lies under a great deal of biblical language. Proverbs states the physical fact and then draws the moral: Surely the churning of milk bringeth forth butter, and the wringing of the nose bringeth forth blood: so the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife (Proverbs 30:33) — three pressures, three inevitable results, and the third is the one being warned against. The nose appears among the ornaments Isaiah strips from the daughters of Zion: The rings, and nose jewels (Isaiah 3:21). It supplies an image of the strength of behemoth, whom no man traps: He taketh it with his eyes: his nose pierceth through snares (Job 40:24). And the Song uses it in a compliment that startles modern readers: thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon which looketh toward Damascus (Song of Solomon 7:4) — the praise is of a bearing that is upright, watchful and unafraid, not of a shape.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines NOSE as the prominent part of the face which is the organ of smell, consisting of two cavities called nostrils; also the end or snout of anything.

expand to see more

NOSE, n. — The prominent part of the face which is the organ of smell, consisting of two cavities called nostrils.

The end of anything; the snout or extremity; as the nose of a bellows.

Scent; sagacity; as a dog with a good nose.

TO LEAD BY THE NOSE, to lead blindly; to cause to follow implicitly.

Anglo-Saxon nosu; Latin nasus; the Hebrew aph means both nostril and anger.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 30:33 — "Surely the churning of milk bringeth forth butter, and the wringing of the nose bringeth forth blood: so the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife."

Isaiah 3:21 — "The rings, and nose jewels,"

Job 40:24 — "He taketh it with his eyes: his nose pierceth through snares."

Song of Solomon 7:4 — "Thy neck is as a tower of ivory; thine eyes like the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bathrabbim: thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon which looketh toward Damascus."

Modern Corruption

Because Hebrew uses one word for nose and for anger, the Old Testament’s language about God’s wrath is bodily and vivid, and it is precisely this that modern discomfort with divine wrath tries to explain away.

expand to see more

Hebrew aph is the nostril, and by the obvious physical association it is also anger — the phrase rendered slow to anger (Psalm 103:8; Nahum 1:3) is literally long of nostril, and the fierceness of his anger is a burning nose. This bodily vocabulary is one of the reasons modern readers find the Old Testament’s wrath language uncomfortable, and it is often handled by declaring such expressions mere anthropomorphism, a concession to primitive minds, behind which lies a God who is not really angry at all. That move costs more than it saves. Wrath in Scripture is not a divine mood but God’s settled and holy opposition to sin, and without it the cross has nothing to accomplish — propitiation means the turning away of wrath (Romans 3:25; 1 John 4:10). The figures are accommodation to our capacity, as Calvin taught; what they express is real.

Proverbs 30:33 is a small masterpiece of practical wisdom. Churn milk and you get butter; wring a nose and you get blood; force wrath and you get strife. The middle image is deliberately crude and physical, so that the third cannot be treated as an accident. Strife does not merely happen; it is produced, by pressure applied, and someone applies it. The verse is a rebuke to the common account of quarrels in which no one is responsible and matters simply escalated. James asks the same question and gives the same answer: whence come wars and fightings? They come of the lusts that war in the members (James 4:1).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew aph (H639), nostril, nose, and by extension anger; nezem (H5141), a ring, worn in the nose or ear; mits (H4330), a pressing or wringing.

expand to see more

Hebrew aph (H639) — the nostril, and so anger; slow to anger is literally long of nostril (Psalm 103:8).

Hebrew mits (H4330) — a squeezing or wringing; the threefold pressure of Proverbs 30:33.

Hebrew nezem (H5141) — a ring worn in the nose or ear; the nose jewels of Isaiah 3:21.

Hebrew appayim — the dual of aph, the two nostrils; the form behind the idiom for patience (Nahum 1:3).

Greek hilasmos (G2434) — propitiation, the turning away of wrath; the New Testament answer to aph.

Usage

"The wringing of the nose bringeth forth blood: so the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife (Proverbs 30:33) — strife is produced, not accidental."

"His nose pierceth through snares (Job 40:24) — the creature no man traps."

"Thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon (Song of Solomon 7:4) — praise of a bearing, upright and watchful."
